concepts.name: Vectors counted, not concepts
concepts.summary: The caveat that occupancy counts active J-lens vectors, which is not the same as counting ideas, because several vectors can together stand for one broader concept.
concepts.explanation: The sparse decomposition reports how many distinct [[j-lens-vector|J-lens vectors]] are active above chance at a position, and the paper states plainly that this is not necessarily the number of concepts or ideas present, since multiple vectors may be used collectively to represent a broader concept. The word-list results give the clearest case: when a list is drawn from one category, the readout fills with the whole word family, and the paper reads this as the model representing a single shared category using the collection of J-lens vectors that constitute it. A count of around 25 vectors is therefore an upper bound on concepts rather than a count of them. This gap between vectors and content is the stated reason for running the [[word-list-experiment|word-list loading experiment]], which measures capacity functionally instead.

concepts.name: Capacity for unrelated words
concepts.summary: With lists of unrelated words, only about six of the words read so far are present in the readout at any comma, and the count stays flat as the list grows.
concepts.explanation: Lists of unrelated words drawn at random are the baseline against which [[category-loading|category loading]] is judged. At each comma, roughly six of the words already read fall in the top-25 readout, and that number does not grow as the list continues to 80 items; words beyond the most recent few simply drop out. This is the paper's headline functional capacity figure for content with no shared theme, and it is measured pooled over the workspace layers. The same measurement at [[single-layer-capacity|a single layer]] gives one or two.

concepts.name: Best rank over the workspace band
concepts.summary: The pooling rule used to score presence: a word's rank is its best rank across the workspace layers L38-92, so a word counts as present if any one of those layers carries it.
concepts.explanation: The list analyses do not read a single layer. For each candidate word they take the best (lowest) [[j-lens-readout|J-lens readout]] rank over the workspace layer range L38-92, and count the word as present if that pooled rank is within the top 25. The choice matters for the numbers reported: pooling this way yields around six unrelated words at once, while repeating the analysis at one layer yields one or two. The paper takes that gap as an indication that the J-space's effective capacity is increased by the ability to store different concepts in different layers, so the pooled figure describes the whole band rather than any single position in it.

concepts.name: Sensitivity to the top-25 cutoff
concepts.summary: A check that the list findings do not depend on the rank cutoff chosen: the count of already-read words is plotted as the threshold $K$ varies, against control words that never appear in the prompt.
concepts.explanation: Counting a word as present when its rank falls within the top 25 is an arbitrary line, so the paper varies it. Panel C of the list figure plots, near the end of the list, how many already-read words fall at rank $K$ or higher as $K$ is swept, alongside a grey curve for control words that never appear in the prompt. The separation between the two curves is what makes a presence count meaningful at any given threshold, and the paper reports that the key qualitative findings are not sensitive to where the threshold is set. The same check is repeated for the [[single-layer-capacity|single-layer]] version of the analysis.

concepts.name: A limit per token position
concepts.summary: The capacity limit applies to what the J-space holds at one token position; attention can still retrieve representations from any earlier position, so the limit does not bound what the model has access to.
concepts.explanation: Every capacity measurement in the paper is taken at a position: occupancy at a position and layer, and list words present at a given comma. The paper notes that this per-position workspace is limited, on the order of tens of concepts, while the model's access to the past is not, because attention can retrieve any internal representation computed earlier in the context at an earlier layer. This relieves the workspace of the need to maintain and propagate state, which the paper contrasts with human working memory, described as sharply limited in capacity and degrading within seconds. One consequence the paper draws is that the contents of a language model's workspace may change more abruptly from token to token than the human workspace does over time.
